content: Distinctive Features of Legionnaires' Disease Clinical Manifestations: Patients typically present with a high-grade fever. A dry cough is a common symptom. Progressive dyspnea, or worsening shortness of breath, is frequently observed. Bronchial breath sounds may be auscultated during a physical examination. In severe cases, adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can develop. Laboratory Abnormalities: A positive Legionella urinary antigen test is a key diagnostic marker. Chest radiographs often reveal alveolar consolidation. Lobar consolidation is another radiographic finding commonly associated with this condition. Distinctive Features of Acute Interstitial Pneumonia Clinical Manifestations: A dry cough is a hallmark symptom. Progressive dyspnea is commonly reported. Adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) may occur in advanced cases. Laboratory Abnormalities: Chest radiographs typically show disseminated consolidation. Interstitial infiltrates are a characteristic finding on imaging. Increased uptake on gallium scans is often observed. Distinctive Features of Mycoplasma Pneumonia Clinical Manifestations: A dry cough is a prominent symptom. Patients may experience pleuritic chest pain. The tympanic membrane may appear inflamed, opaque, and hypomobile upon examination. Bronchial breath sounds are often noted during auscultation. Laboratory Abnormalities: Lymphocytosis is a common laboratory finding. Cold agglutinins are frequently positive. Chest radiographs may show alveolar consolidation, interstitial infiltrates, or lobar consolidation. Distinctive Features of Pneumococcal Pneumonia Clinical Manifestations: Hemoptysis, or coughing up blood, is a notable symptom. Fine rales may be heard on auscultation. Pleuritic chest pain is frequently reported. Increased breath sounds and bronchial breath sounds are common findings. Dullness on chest percussion is often present. Patients may produce purulent sputum. Shallow respiration and pectoriloquy are observed in some cases. Increased tactile fremitus and egophony are additional clinical signs. A productive cough and high-grade fever are typical. Laboratory Abnormalities: Pleural effusion, often exudative, is a common finding. Respiratory alkalosis may be detected. Parenchymal hyperlucency is sometimes seen on chest radiographs. Gallium scans may show increased uptake. Unilateral diaphragm elevation can be observed on imaging. Alveolar and lobar consolidation are characteristic radiographic findings. Gram-positive diplococci are identified on sputum Gram stain. Distinctive Features of Pneumocystis Carinii Pneumonia (PCP) Clinical Manifestations: This condition is often seen in immunosuppressed individuals. Mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema may develop. A hacking cough is a common symptom. Progressive dyspnea is frequently reported. Laboratory Abnormalities: Respiratory alkalosis is a typical finding. Serum beta-D-glucan levels are elevated. Chest radiographs may show alveolar consolidation, lobar consolidation, or interstitial infiltrates. Distinctive Features of Pulmonary Embolism Clinical Manifestations: Patients may report calf pain or swelling, indicative of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Decreased pulse pressure is a common finding. Dyspnea with a normal chest X-ray is a key diagnostic clue. Hemoptysis and hyperventilation are frequently observed. Immobility and a history of prior DVT are significant risk factors. An increased pulmonic component of the heart sound may be auscultated. Pleuritic chest pain and substernal chest pain are common complaints. Pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular heave, and right ventricular hypertrophy may develop. A right-to-left shunt can occur in severe cases. Tachypnea and unilateral lower extremity edema are often present. Venous stasis and thrombophlebitis are additional risk factors. Laboratory Abnormalities: Atrial fibrillation may be detected on ECG. Bone fractures and atelectasis may be seen on imaging. Chest radiographs may reveal lobar consolidation, a prominent pulmonary artery, or Hampton's hump. Elevated D-dimer levels are a key diagnostic marker. Echocardiography may show right ventricular enlargement or a thrombus. Hypocapnia and hypoxia are common findings. Lung scans may reveal segmental perfusion defects or ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch. Pleural effusion, which may be exudative or bloody, is often present. Right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) may be seen on ECG. Distinctive Features of Streptococcal Pneumonia Clinical Manifestations: Pectoriloquy and bronchial breath sounds are common findings. Empyema and erythema nodosum may develop. Purulent sputum is frequently produced. Shallow respiration and increased tactile fremitus are observed. Pleuritic chest pain and egophony are common symptoms. Laboratory Abnormalities: Respiratory alkalosis is a typical finding. Pleural effusion, often exudative, is a common complication. Gallium scans may show increased uptake. Gram-positive cocci in chains are identified on sputum Gram stain. Alveolar and lobar consolidation are characteristic radiographic findings. Distinctive Features of Viral Pneumonia Clinical Manifestations: Pleuritic chest pain and bronchial breath sounds are common. Influenza-like symptoms are frequently reported. Fine rales and bronchovesicular breath sounds may be auscultated. Laboratory Abnormalities: Lymphocytosis is a common laboratory finding. Respiratory alkalosis may be detected. Chest radiographs may show lobar consolidation or interstitial infiltrates.
